newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banks setting up domestic Sfr repo market.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks setting up domestic Sfr repo market.

text.p: Swiss banks are establishing a market for Swiss franc securities repurchase, or "repo" agreements, after tax authorities agreed to end a stamp tax on such business at the start of 1997, bankers here said.

"The decision by the tax authorities to abolish the stamp duty was taken very quickly, after several rounds of discussions," Frederik Vornholt, head of SBC Warburg's securities lending desk for Switzerland, said in an interview.

He said that SBC's knowledge of the securities lending business, already well-established in Switzerland, had helped SBC to build up the repo business rapidly in a short time and to participate in an expanding market.
As to prospects for volume, he said: "At the moment it is premature to give estimates on volume, but I can assure you that reputable institutions have already shown their interest."
A repo deal is a two-way transaction in which one party borrows funds on a short-term basis from a second, using securities such as federal bonds as collateral.
Repos have long been used in the U.S., where Treasury debt serves as collateral for short-term loans, often used to refinance positions in the government debt market.

There is also an active repo market in London. German banks recently created a stir when they announced they would repatriate deutschmark repo trading to Frankfurt, after the Bundesbank ended its minimum reserve requirements.
At the same time, at least one Swiss bank is considering moving its Bund-based repo business to London.
Swiss banks have been involved in domestic securities lending since 1990. But until the stamp tax decision, repo business denominated in Swiss francs has been non-existent.
Bankers are unsure how the repo business will evolve in future, however, given that there is still a 35 percent Swiss withholding tax imposed on non-banks in such transactions.

For example, if a broker firm in London were seeking to take up cash via a repo, the repo interest payment to the broker, classified as the holder of the bond, would be subject to the 35 percent withholding tax.
Through double-taxation agreements, most of the money would be recovered eventually but it meanwhile earns no interest in the period in which it is withheld.
A spokesman for the federal tax authorities in Berne said there are no plans to make changes to the withholding tax, which brings Berne around two to three billion francs in annual revenues.

Bankers here also said that unlike the U.S. market, where the division between banks and brokerages leaves brokers with no alternative but to borrow to finance securities deals, in Switzerland the banks are well supplied with liquidity from their retail deposits.
Smaller firms, however, may see repos as a short-term credit tool.
According to bankers here, some Swiss banks may also prefer to take up liquidity in the repo market and use their customer deposits for other investments.
Hedge funds also could look to Swiss repos to refinance their holdings in the Swiss debt market.

Another problem is lack of a highly liquid government cash bond market in Switzerland, although the Swiss Treasury has been building larger benchmark tranches in recent years. It is also said to be looking to improve liquidity for short-term Treasury bills, or money market claims (GMBF).

Swiss banks are also seeking to establish a standardised contract for repos. U.K. repo markets look to the Global Master Repurchase Agreement (GMRA) based on guidelines set by the U.S. Public Securities Association (PSA) and International Securities Market Association (ISMA). Swiss tax authorities also favour the agreement as a basis for Swiss repos.

But bankers said that there are some areas where the agreement does not conform to Swiss repurchase deals, citing complications pertaining to the Swiss withholding tax, and its treatment of dividends or coupon payments on securities used in repo transactions.
